withheld_text: What if the zeros were a spectrum?
Compare unfolded zero gaps with a random-matrix ensemble and an uncorrelated reference.
Reproducible seed 20260926 · eight independent matrix draws
Hψρ = zρψρ, ψρ ≠ 0, zρ = (ρ − ½)/i · proposed spectral identification

Hilbert–Pólya proposal: seek a self-adjoint operator H with a proved identification of its eigenvalues, including multiplicities, with zρ = (ρ − ½)/i for all nontrivial zeros ρ. Such an identification would make every zρ real and imply RH. No such self-adjoint spectral realization has been established. Merely matching the real ordinates γ = Im ρ does not imply RH.

For the symmetrized dilation operator H0 = −i(x d/dx + ½), initially on Cc∞(0, ∞) in L²((0, ∞), dx), the deficiency indices are (0, 0). Its self-adjoint closure has purely absolutely continuous spectrum ℝ; it does not supply the required discrete zero spectrum.
The matrix samples here follow GUE eigenvalue statistics. They are random comparison spectra, not an operator that proves RH.
Unfolding removes the changing average spacing. The first ten zeros are omitted; the remaining small sample still has substantial finite-height effects.
Rows are separate ensembles, not a physical dimension. A low density near gap zero indicates level repulsion. The Poisson reference peaks at zero because independent levels can be arbitrarily close.
Gaps below half the mean: zeta 6.7% · GUE 10.3% · Poisson 39.3% (theoretical). Small finite samples fluctuate; resemblance does not identify an RH operator.
Gap s divided by its mean · density, not counts · bins of width 0.2 · plot range 0 ≤ s ≤ 3.
Each line is a computed real eigenvalue. The middle 60% contributes to the spacing comparison.

withheld_text: RH Field: particle flows that come back to RH.

Particles follow three numerically evaluated fields built from ζ and ξ; a finite model of the zero dynamics of the de Bruijn–Newman family; five physics bridges (Berry–Keating xp, Landau levels, Lee–Yang zeros, the primon gas, a driven qubit); three fields of phase 3 (ζ as a Maxwell field, the zeros as a Coulomb gas, a superconducting symmetry class against L-function families); and two of phase 4 (the truncations of ζ against the continued function, and the ideal Bose gas). Phase 5 draws 3D stream tubes; its first preset, the Burgers vortex, is a reference picture with no link to RH, and its second lifts the Newton flow to 3D, a construction with no RH claim. Every preset carries its link type to RH (theorem, exact reformulation, model, analogy or contrast), states the connection, has a control, and says what its picture does and does not show. No physics here proves or tests RH.

What this field says about RH

A strip around a line of unit charges at unfolded positions x (mean spacing 1). The ζ set places them at the unfolded ordinates of the first 1000 zeros (computed with mpmath.zetazero, data/field/zeta-zeros-1000.json; the Explorer’s 100-zero table if that file cannot be loaded). Particles follow the 2D Coulomb field of the charges. The strip uses x = N̄(γ), y = (σ − ½)·N̄′(γ). These coordinates unfold the ordinates and use the same local scale transversely at the critical line. The displayed field is the Coulomb field of the selected unfolded charges. It reproduces their local charge singularities, but is not an exact coordinate transform of ζ′/ζ. Switch the charges to a GUE sample (β = 2) or a GOE sample (β = 1) — each 8 seeded matrices of size 200, central 120 levels of each kept: 960 levels in eight segments — or to independent Poisson points (as many as the ζ set, one segment); “Animate” runs Dyson Brownian motion on one 64-level GUE matrix, whose stationary law is the β = 2 log-gas (the histograms and numerical comparisons stay those of the fixed comparison sample). The side plot shows the pair correlation R2(u) against the limiting curve 1 − (sin πu/πu)², and the nearest-neighbour spacing density against the Wigner surmises.

Montgomery (1973): Assuming RH, the high-height pair-correlation measure for distinct zero indices has the limiting density 1 − (sin πu/πu)² when tested against suitable functions whose Fourier transforms are supported in (−1, 1). The unrestricted pair-correlation statement is conjectural. The finite histograms shown here are comparisons with that limiting curve. Odlyzko’s computations of zeros at great heights agree with the GUE predictions to high precision. The GUE form is the “quantum chaos” heuristic (Berry; Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit) behind Hilbert–Pólya: the ordinates look like the spectrum of a chaotic quantum system without time-reversal symmetry. The electrostatics is exact for the matrices: the GUE eigenvalue density ∝ Π|xi − xj|² e−Σx²/2 is the Boltzmann weight of a 2D Coulomb (log-)gas on a line at β = 2 (Dyson, 1962). Maxwell link: in the appropriate flat-cavity regime below the first transverse cutoff, the relevant Maxwell mode reduces to a two-dimensional Helmholtz problem; suitable chaotic microwave billiards exhibit GOE-type statistics when time reversal is preserved and GUE-type statistics when a ferrite breaks it (So, Anlage, Ott, Oerter, PRL 1995 [unverified here]) — a statistical physical comparison, not a statement about the real parts of ζ’s zeros. Statistics cannot prove RH: ordinate statistics alone do not determine the real parts of zeros.
C6 · spectral statistics (Hilbert–Pólya heuristic); spacing histogram of zeros 11–100 also in module 05 Spectral Lab

Replace the selected on-line zero by the off-line pair ρ, 1 − ρ̄ (the phase 1 δ and zero choice). Both have ordinate γ₀, so replacing the one on-line entry by two entries at the same ordinate inserts one exact zero spacing. The readout reports the largest bin changes of R2 and of the spacing density and the change in RMS distance to the sine-kernel curve, next to the differences between two seeded GUE comparison samples, each containing 960 retained levels in eight segments (the ζ set is one segment of 1000 levels, or 100 with the fallback table). This is an illustrative comparison, not a calibrated detection threshold. Or switch the charges to Poisson points for comparison.

The 1000 unfolded ordinates sit 0.086 (rms) from the sine-kernel curve 1 − (sin πu/πu)² and 0.366 from Poisson; their spacings 0.061 from the GUE surmise and 0.386 from e^(−s). The displayed histogram shows suppressed small spacings, consistent with the GUE heuristic; this is not a proof.

This is a statistical analogy. No self-adjoint spectral realization identifying all zρ = (ρ − ½)/i, with multiplicity, has been established. Agreement with GUE statistics neither constructs such an operator nor proves that every zρ is real; self-adjointness alone does not require GUE statistics. The first 1000 zeros are at low height, ending near γ = 1419.4. In the standard finite-height pair-correlation model, the leading smooth correction after the specified unfolding has scale 1/log²(γ/2π). This is a model asymptotic, not a certified error bound for these histograms; finite sample size, binning and unfolding also affect the comparison. Montgomery’s theorem needs RH and restricted Fourier support. Matrix samples are 8 matrices of size 200 (the central 60 %, 120 levels each, 960 in all, kept; semicircle unfolding), seeded and reproducible. The So–Anlage et al. citation is from memory [unverified here].

Ring k holds (2k − 1)² < n ≤ (2k + 1)², and (2k + 1)² sits at (k, −k). A diagonal of the grid carries 4j² + Bj + C in its step index j, with B even; the cell under the pointer shows its integer n.

Dense diagonals are a property of quadratic polynomials and residue classes, not a hidden pattern in the primes. The polar arms are arithmetic progressions; these lines are quadratic sequences, a different mechanism.

Of C = 6.6408, the primes dividing W = 30 give 2.000 · 1.500 · 1.250 = 3.7500; the coprime-to-W control reproduces that part of the enrichment and not the rest. Relative to a C = 1 line, f is richer by the factor C because of its roots modulo small primes: residue classes, not a hidden pattern in the primes.

Straight diagonal runs (≥ 4 cells): n = 40 … 172 step 2, 67 cells ↙, 4j² + 162j + 1681 in its step index j (checked against the grid ✓); n = 39 … 171 step 2, 67 cells ↗, 4j² + 158j + 1601 in its step index j (checked against the grid ✓). Outside these runs the values of f are not on one diagonal: the polynomial of a line holds segment by segment.

The Bateman–Horn conjecture (Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture F for quadratics) predicts #{n ≤ x : f(n) prime} ≈ C(f) Σ 1/log f(n), with C(f) = ∏p (1 − ω(p)/p)/(1 − 1/p) and ω(p) the number of roots of f mod p. It is unproved for every polynomial of degree 2: nobody has shown that n² + 1 is prime infinitely often. C is computed here as an Euler product over p ≤ 10⁶; the values at p ≤ 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶ are listed with C, and their spread indicates, but does not bound, the error. A prime p with ω(p) = p divides every value (a fixed prime divisor), so C = 0. A reducible f factors, and Bateman–Horn does not apply.

Polar spiral on the Riemann sphere
One residue class a mod q
SYNTHETIC control: Cramér random set (seed 2026) in place of the primes

P(n) = n^β (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ) with θ = φ = αn. At β = 1, α = 1 this is the picture (p sin p cos p, p sin² p, p cos p). β = 0 puts every point on the unit sphere, on Viviani’s curve. The arms come from αn mod 2π: q steps of α nearly close a turn when q = 44 (44 ≈ 7 · 2π), so n and n + 44 land close together.
The Cramér set keeps each n ≥ 3 with probability 1/log n (seeded, reproducible). It has about as many members as the primes but ignores divisibility: compare which arms it fills.
Rotate with drag · scroll to zoom · arrow keys rotate

RH IN THIS VIEW This picture is about how primes p are spread mod 2π (equidistribution, a Weyl–Vinogradov statement), not about zeros of ζ. RH enters only through the error terms of prime counts in residue classes (GRH for L(s, χ)); nothing here tests RH.
Up: z = n^β cos θ · across: x · depth: −y · scaled by 1.1/N^β
Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom
Colour: class n mod 44 · violet: the direction curve on the rim sphere (Viviani’s curve) · amber: the double ray through (0, 1, 0) · white: the cone’s vertex
π(N; q, a) over reduced a (min – max)

Count of drawn integers in each class a mod 44. Mint: a coprime to q; amber: a sharing a factor with q, which a prime can occupy only when it divides q. Primes fill φ(q) = 20 classes; all integers and the SYNTHETIC Cramér set fill all 44.

Histogram of αn mod 2π in 72 bins over the uniform level (dashed = 1). Grey dashes: the density predicted from the arms of q* = 710 alone (710α ≈ 113·2π, so by N they turn only 0.008 rad), keeping only the φ(q*) = 280 classes a prime can use; correlation with the histogram 0.86. The dips for primes are arithmetic, not noise: the missing classes of q* have not yet turned far enough to average out. Vinogradov’s theorem says the histogram flattens as N → ∞.

Each point is n^β times a unit vector u(θ, φ). With θ = φ = αn, u runs along Viviani’s curve, the figure-eight where the cylinder x² + (y − ½)² = ¼ meets the unit sphere; so the points lie on the cone over that curve, at distance n^β from its vertex. The hourglass pinch is where the cone’s vertex and its double ray (through (0, 1, 0), where the curve crosses itself) project. Nothing is iterated and nothing is sensitive to its input: each point is a closed formula in n, so despite any resemblance this is not a Lorenz-type attractor or chaos. Each point is n^β times a unit vector u(θ, φ). With θ = φ = αn, u runs along Viviani’s curve, the figure-eight where the cylinder x² + (y − ½)² = ¼ meets the unit sphere; so the points lie on the cone over that curve, at distance n^β from its vertex. The hourglass pinch is where the cone’s vertex and its double ray (through (0, 1, 0), where the curve crosses itself) project. Nothing is iterated and nothing is sensitive to its input: each point is a closed formula in n, so despite any resemblance this is not a Lorenz-type attractor or chaos. The arms come from αn mod 2π: q = 44 steps of α are 7 turns plus Δ = 1.77e-2, so the 44 classes a mod q give 44 slowly turning arms; primes fill the φ(q) = 20 classes coprime to q, plus one point for each prime dividing q. The SYNTHETIC Cramér set fills every class: the arms themselves come from the angle, the missing arms from divisibility.
